Our attention has been called hy an article in one of the provincial news papers, to a very important mechanical invention for which a patent has recently been granted to Scotch gentlemen, and which promises to effect a greater and more beneficial change in the working of machinery than lias taken place since the brilliant discoveries of Watt. The two great drawbacks of the steam engine (besides i lie large space it occupies) have been the bulk, and the consequent expense of the fuel which it requires, ihe latter preventing us application to many purposes for which it would otherwise have been a most elective agent; and the foimer impeding Us locomotive energy, and confining it, particularly as regards navigation, within comparatively narrow limits. Any reduction in either of these respects is thereby obviously so much clear gain. 1 lie invention to which we allude promises to effect a prodigious saving in both, hy diminishing the expenditure of fuel to somewhat less than one fifth of what is now required for au equal degree of power. It has already, we are informed, been put to the test by the construction of au engine of about 20 horse power, which has for some time been driving all the machinery of an extensive foundry with no larger consumption than we have just mentioned, and with every prospect of a considerably greater reduction being effected hy some slight changes in the details. The motive power used is the common

atmospheric air ; and another great advantage of the new engine arises from a saving of space equal to wliat is usually occupied hy die furnace and boilers of a steam engine. If these things he so, it is impossible to calculate the results to which so important a discovery must lead þÿ Morning Chronicle.

In France, llie court und people seem to be wholly occupied with the approaching trial of Quenisset, which is ordered to take place on Monday or Tuesday, the 6th and 7th of December There is something worthy of observation, not only in the different forms of French and English trials, but still more so in the preliminary proceedings. In England, the practice is that an indictment for treason must, like all other criminal indictments, go before a grand jury, and be there found and sent up to the higher court. In France, it seems that it would be imprudent to trust matters of treason to the discretion or public feeling of their juries, and such indictments, therefore, are sent in the first instance to the Chamber of Peers. A further circumstance worthy of note in this affair of Quenisset, and in the evidence and examination which have already been made public, is the total corruption, not only of all moral feeling, but even of the veiv understanding and judgment, which pervades so large a portion of ihe French populace þÿ In England, indeed, we have our chartists and Oweuiles, and a set of misguided blackguards who seem to have lost all faculty of distinguishing right from wrong, and truth from error; whose very mental vision appears to be gone, and who thus wander about in total and unconscious blindness, not knowing to what irretrievable ruin and self destruction their paths are leading them. But in England this total blindness and depravity are confined within a very small class The

public feeding as well as the public judgment are entirely against them, and being thus overwhelmed hv numbers, and watched and restrained on all sides, their faculty of doing mischief is of little account. But in France this wretched depravation of the heart and understanding seems to pervade the great majority of the populace. Secret societies seem to exist in all their large towns, arid the horrible doctrines of community of goods, community of women, the abolition of marriage, the redivision of the lands, the overthrow ot government, and the assassination of the royal family, are embodied in so many distinct resolutions, and form the secret compact ot these affiliated societies. The next point in foreign affairs is that of Spain, and the two present critical circumstances in Spanish affairs are the democratic or rather Jacobin condition of Baiceluna, and the order of the Begem to demolish, without loss of time, all the forts and castles in Biscay, and Navarre By the last accounts from Barcelona it apjiears that the revolutionary juntas had all taken flight, and had proceeded to France upon their road towards England. On the following day the .r>ih of the current month. General Van Halen, þÿEspartero gene- s ral, had entered the city, and all parties had submitted to him, the National Guards only retaining their arms, but signifying their readiness to obey his orders. From the St. Thomas Times, January 5, 1842, ARRIVAL OF A ROYAL MAIL STEAMER. The Steamer Forth, Lieut. Fayrer, R N. Commander, from Southampton bound to Nassau, New Providence, unexpectedly came

inel. She sailed from England on the 17th of last month thus performing the vovage in something less than seventeen days. We have the gratification of announcing the þÿ þÿForth to be one of the 14 Liners destined to ply regularly between this and Europe, the arrival of which forms a memorable era in the annals of the Western World. We are enabled through the courteous and gentlemanly civilities received whilst on a visit to this vessel, to record our unbounded admiration of the noble specimen of Naval Aichitecture which graces our harbour. The style, order, and elegance, which exists in every department, and the particular attention which appears to have been taken to secure all tending to the convenience and comforts of passengers of different sexes. ! We are called upon on this occasion, to express an appropriate tribute to gigantic conception. The profound genius ; and the liberal enterprize of a Nation affording to the world at large so proud a monument of Industry and the perfection of science. The importance of their application ; the magnitude of enterprize exceeds any thing ever recorded in maritime History. We view these Steamers as a connecting link which bind us to Europe- We cease from henceforth to be strangers and are now made neighbours. þÿ They are the medium through which time and space are conquered. The means of fellowship and community of intercourse ; and of general advantage to civilization. We conclude these brief remarks with the best wishes for the prosperity of the þÿ þÿForth

its respected Commander, and officers, and hope that the result of this Brilliant undertaking may prove in the end as successful as the nature of the enterprize is glorious, thus I fulfilling to the utmost extent the flattering ex- I pectations of the noble projectors.

The earthquake was so sudden, that those persons who escaped, had hardly time to get out of their houses before the falling ol the walls. In a second, the Department ot Cartago has become a total ruin. The destruction is so great, that the site of any particular edifice is hardly to be distinguished among the ruins- In the citv, the houses, even to the stone work, were thrown upwards bv the shock, and fell down again in heaps of rubbish. Inhabitants of Costa Rica ! þÿ At half past six this morning, a terrific earthquake totaily ruined the Department ot Cartago, and caused most terrible ravages in San Jose, leaving eom paratively uninjured the other departments of the State. The latter, particularly, are under obligations to succor their unlortunate fellowcitizens of the former, who have suffered to such a degree, that there is hardly a straw shed left to shelter them from the rigor of the season. The city of San Jose, which has suffered also in the common disaster, will lend all the aid in her power to those of the unfortunates who may come to take refuge with her ; and on the part of the Government all the assistance it can give will he afforded. People of Costa- Rica ! þÿ You are all of one family. The misfortunes which are suffered by any portion should be, and in fact are, felt in common. Hospitality has always been a distinguishing feature among you ; but now, more than ever, must you manifest to the world that you truly possess that virtue. Be generous, and extend a protecting hand to the afflicted. Hasten to aid them þÿ build up sheds to protect their families from the weather þÿ carry them provisions, and feed their helpless children, who weep lor tfie loss of their parents þÿ take thern to your hauses, and give ear to those who ask your charity. It is a duty, and you will fulfil it. You will thus strengthen those bands of friendship w hich unite the whole State in a single brotherhood þÿ San Jose,

B. CARILLO. þÿ WM©W» Giiffith's Cotton þÿFloater yesterday We announced the arrival of Mr. G. R Griffith, with 93 hales of cotton, enveloped in his new- ly invented " Cotton Floater ," or India Hubher Bags. This is the first experiment of his invention, and the result is such as to satisfy him of its great utility and perfect success. Not only he, but we believe all who have seen the cotton and the " Floaters," since their arrival, are lully satisfied that the invention will answer the most sanguine expectations of the enterprising inventor. The cotton belongs to Dr. Earl, and was shipped from his plantation on the Tombigbee river. The process of shipping is very simple. You have onlv to envelope each bale in one of the India Rubber bags, throw them into the water, lash them together with ropes, and set them afloat. These 93 hales came to our market most beautiful order, perfectly dry, in and sound. The bales are large, weighing between five and six hundred pounds, and yet, the raft, as it may be called, diew not

more than three and a half inches water. In this respect Mr. Griffith was agreeably disappointed, as he expected it would draw considerably more. We are perfectly satisfied that the invention is destined to he of incalculable benefit to the planters in tiie vicinity of streams not navigable for steamboats ; and we have no doubt the " Floaters" will soon he in general use on the Goosa, Cahawha, Black Warrior, Little Bigbv, Noxubee, & other small streams We have heretofore describt d the " Floater" more particularly, and it is unnecessary to repeat the description. We would earnestly recommend the invention to the l'ianters of Alabama, as eminently worthy of their attention. Mr. Griffith will still further test the utility of the ' Floaters" on other and smaller streams, in the course of the ensuing winter. þÿ Mobile Advertiser.

At my last visit to Leipsi 1 understood that matters were going on badly with homaeopathy, which indeed is now hut little heard of in Germany and France, and only required to be understood by the pubiic for its absurdity to be apparent, though there will always be credulous individuals who are to be caught by any novelty, when presented uncier a specious appearance, and backed by an unintelligible name. establishment of dispensaries, which, 1 be. lieve. the only one that remains i-. the above mentioned at Leipsic, even if it be still in existence. for a few months before my arrival the house physician having become convinced, during a residence ot some time in the dispensary, of the nullity and danger of hoþÿ myopathy, gave up appointment, his and published an exposition of the system pur tied» witfi an account of cases, which clearly shows þÿ what had long been evident to the bulk of the profession and the public þÿ that the so-called cures were recoveries from ordinary ailments by the efforts of nature, which were frequently a long time tinder treatment, whereas, by a proper medication and attention at ihe outset, they might probablv have been removed in a few days, and lhat manv of the more serious cases got worse instead of belter, for the want of active treatment. It must not be supposed that the homaeopathists always adhere to the principles of the doctrine. If has not unfrequenth happened that persons who attributed their re-

covery to homanopathy were treated allopathically without, their being aware of it. In 'act, one practitioner in Leipsic, a professed homacopalhist, candidly acknowledged that he pursued both plans of treatment, and was accustomed to ask his patients by which method they would be treated, as both were " equally good We suspect that all homaeopathists are not equally candid. (From the Morning Chronicle) iiord Ashburton's appointment has been favourably received in commercial circles, and given a tone of confidence to the holders of state stocks. (From the Times,) l he selection of Lord Ashburton for this delicate mission appears to us, upon the whole, to be deserving of commendation. With immense mercantile interests extending over the whole þÿworld interests which, while peculiarly idemified with America, cannot suffer interruption in any quarter without incurtinga serious injury in their entire range, his lordship has the advantage of proceeding to the United Stales, not only with the highest claims upon the consideration of that trading community, hut with a direct personal concern in the maintenance of general peace- Thus, while the independence and integrity of Lord Ashburton place him above the suspicion ot unduly yielding to extravagant, demands which he can well afford to resist, his loi dship s large and intimate connexion with American commerce may naturally be suppose.) to deter him from all such petty sticklings as may obviously tend to interrupt it. The noble lord, moreover, is thoroughly acquainted with the whole question touching the right ol search, as affecting arnongall nations, the perfectly compatible interests of humanity and tiade.

The foreign intelligence of the past week, þÿ that portion which lias arrived from foreign quarters. þÿ bears so immediately upon British interests, and, indeed, so wholly turns upon them, as to supersede all such intelligence nearer home ; the affairs of China Anglia mstan. and Persia, aie now the actual fields of British conflict, and engage the solicitude of all persons, whilst the affairs ot France ana the Levant sink into comparative insignificance, I he extraordinary expres-, which arrived overland from India, at the end of last week, brought dispatches from China up to October the 10th. and from Bombay to November the 30th ; that is, six weeks from India, and three months from China which may therefore be assumed as the average period within winch we may receive all future dispatches from Bombay, As the proceedings of our expedition are related with sufficient clearness and brevity in Sir H. þÿPottinger circular, s wh.ch will be found in another part of our paper, it is unnecessary to repeat them in ibis place. It appears that when the last accounts were sent off the expedition was about to take possession of Chusun and Ningpo. In our former papers we have given a sufficient account of Chusan and its position. Nmgpo is a largo city about half way between Amoy and Pekin. It is a city greatly valued by the Chinese, being at once rich and populous, and one of the great emporiums which supply Pekin. But we should doubt whether we have sufficient

land force to spare at present from our ulterior objects to maintain possession of it ; we shall probably act as we did at Amoy, capture, dismantle it. and then leave a ship or two on the station, and proceed forward.
Indeed, according to present appearances, it would seem as il we must prepare to carry on the war upon a large scale, and that more ships and soldiers must lie sent from Eiiglaud to India.

wait From the Britannia, London Januaiy 1, 184ii. j FRANCE. Louis Philippe opened the Session in person on Monday, at one o'clock. His Majesty went in a close carriage, drawn by four horses, and attended by four other carriages. Extraordinary precautions had been taken to prevent the approach of any person within musket-shot of the line of march, except the military on duty ; even the terraces of the Tuileries gardens were closed. The King opened the Session of the Cham bers with the usual formalities, and delivered the following Speech from the Throne : þÿ vouis, and the Gentlemen, Peers, and Deputies : Since the close of your last session, the questions which excited in the East o tr just solicitude have reached their term. 1 have concluded with the Emperor of Austria, the ! Queen of Great Britain, the King ofPmssia, the Emperor of Russia, and the Multan, a convention which consecrates the common intention of the Powers to maintain the peace ofEuiope. and consolidate the repose of the Ottoman empire. The great burdens imposed upon the country have already experienced considerable reductions. It would have been my liv<|y wish that a balance should have been immediately re-established between the expenditure and revenues of the .State. This is the result which we must now prepare, and which you will achieve without weakening our military organisation, and without deferring the execu- i tion of those works which are to mcreast the national prosperity. j A project of law will be presented to vou for constructing the principal lines of a gieat

system of railroads calcu'ated to ensure those rapid and easy communications with all parts of our territory, which will prove a source of force and riches to the nation I am endeavouring at the same lime, bv negotiations prudently conducted, to extend our commercial relations, and to open new markets for the productions of our soil, and of our arts. Such labours honour peace, and render it stable and fruitlul at the same time I hive reason to reckon that it will not be Histuibed, receiving from all the Powers the most amicable assurances. I have taken measures to prevent any external complication from disturbing the s curit v of our African possessions. ( hubrave soldiers are pursuing on that land, henceforth ami for ever French, the course of their noble labours in which 1 am happy that my sons have had the honour of concurring. Our perseverance shall complete the work undertaken by our courageous army, and France will introduce j into Algeria hercivilisatiunas the consequence of iier glory. The financial law's and others, having for their object to introduce useful improvements in the public administration, will he presented to you immediately. Whatever may he the burdens of ottr situs tion, France would support them without difficulty if faction did not unceasingly ohsti uct the course of her powerful activity I will not dwell upon the intrigues ami crimes of the factious : hut let us not forget, gentlemen, that it is that which debars our country from fully enjoying all the blessings which Providence
lias conferred upon it, and which retards the development of that legal and pacific liberty

iionsms atisl which France has at last achieved, and of which I make it my glory to ensure her the possession. We shall follow up this task, gentlemen. My Go. eminent will do its duty. It will maintain everywhere and constantly the authority of the laws, and cause them to he respected, as it will respect tnem itselt. Your loyal support will aid me. In enlightening the country with persevering sincerity with I regard to its true interest, we shall strengthen by its support, and by our union keep entire, the sacred deposit of order and public liberties which the Charter iias confided to us. Future generations will reap the fruit of our etideagratitude of our country will be our recompense.

SPEECH OF THE KING OF THE FRENCH. Tite speech of Louis Philippe on opening the Session of the Chamheis on AloiMtay last, is a clear and manly document. Its first paragraph states that a convention has been concluded between England, Austria. Prussia, Russia, the Sultan, and France, pledging the seveial Powers to maintain the peace ol Europe, and consoituale the repose of tiie Ottoman þÿempire. 'J his is a great point gained for the t anqoiiitv of the wot id, and a formidable blow I t>> tile factious spirit which in France itselt lias been so long urging w at, simply as a pretext for domestic revolution. The Algerine war has been to I cu ts Philippe what the Spanish war was to Napoleon þÿ þÿ an ulcer and the longer it is carneb on, the more fatal will oe its results þÿ Pius paragraph pledge- France to its continuance ; and this war will yet bring misery upon France Nothing astonishes rational men more than to see the ittde effect which the most solemn evidences of the wrath of Provo), nee against unjust wats produce on tlie minds of men in possession ol large power, i o France, ol all the nations of the earth, lai terrible lesson has been the most immediately directed. The twice taken capital, the twice-conquered country, the twice captured Emperor, even the twice-buned hones ol dial Emperor, ought to have taught her to iienible at the name of inilitaiy rapine. þÿ Such was the punishment fin her outbreak against Europe. Even the Algerine war had its singular and impressive seal of Divine

vengeance, in the utter ruin of ail its leading agents. It destroyed the Bourbon King, the Bou bon succession, and sent the whole Royal Family into retutnless banishment. It destroyed the Government, and sent the whole Ministry into the dungeon or into exile, ftom which, hi either case, they have emerged only to remain in total obscuiity. It stripped M aiimont, the Minister of War, ol Ins Country, in an instant, and sent him a wanderer tluough the world; it ruined Booumont, the commander ol the invasion, and sent linn, too, a w anderer through the wot Id. Thus, the whole of the chief advisers and nctois were stricken. We ask, whether anything more decisive, or more demonstrative of a high purpose, can he conceived ? Nor was the punishment put oil to a lime when its connexion with the mime might have been forgotten; it followed instantly. With the fiisi blood shed on the soil of Algiers, the vengeance came, and the King and Ins Government were swept away, as if they were swept Indore the wind. Of the troops, the mere instruments, the fate may he more obscure. But how few

of those ever saw France again ? Africa fiat already cost 100,000 fives, and what have been the fruits ? The French talk of giory ; they should he ashamed to use the word, when their only antagonists are the half ai med peasants of a wilderness, and their only conquests are dilapidated villages, fetid swamps, and boundless sands Algiers, to this hour, acts only as a drain for French blood and French gold it has never returned, and will never return, the millionth part of the money that has been tiuiig atvav in its deserts.

From the Jamaica Morning Journal þÿ, January 11, On Saturday last we briefly adverted to the arrival of H iVI Schooner Hide, from Carthagena, and now furnish our readers witlt such further details as we have learnt, of the highly important intelligence brought b\ her. As they are already aware, immediately on the information reaching Cartliagena, of the villainous outrage committed l>v Carmona's merciless adherents on the British vessels Little William and Jane and Sarah, as well as the British subjects on board. H. M. Brig Clmrybdis, Lieut lie Courev, sailed in quest of the tyrants squadron, to seek reparation for the wanton insult offered towards i our flag. On t fie 15th Uec., site, together with the ' government naval forces, which had also gone out to attack the enemv, fell in with their flotilla off Zispota, and an engagement took place, which after about half an hour's duration, terminated in favour of the Charvbdis. and her coadjutors. Five of the rebel j vessels, viz ; the Bug Marcelino, and the j Schooners Caroline, Sirena, Tolima and Henrietta became prizes to the victors, whilst the Schooner Boyaea, whose hull was much riddled with shot went down. The news ol this signal success speedily reached Car- j thagena, wheie it created one universal sen- t timeut of rejoicing, which, however, was ! damped on the 20th Dec h\ the capture and possession (supposed to have been effected bv treachery) of the Suburb of J unani, by Carmona's gun boats. This event has naturally effected the Carthagcnians. but private advi

ces represent this (bishop as of roinpnrr«five!y trivial consequence, and cornmnnicate the resolute determination of the entire City to lie buried in its ruins sooner than surrender to i the beseigers. What renders this contretemps more to he regretted, is the fact, that ' Carmona bud only resolved the day previous to its occurrence on raising the siege as a hopeless case, and retiring to la Cienega, giving orders that a last attack should be made that evening as an expiring effort.

Carthagena is stated to be much ruined and damaged from the galling fire continually pouring into it, the destruction of property therein, being 'estimated at not less than one hundred thousand dollars. During the þÿI rent'll invasion ol Egypt, Bonaparte visited Suez, with the view ol restoring its old hat bon i and of ascertaining the site and rou'e of the Canal. The levels were taken, and an iaborute memoir prepared upon the subject by the Engineer Ltq.ete. Had Napoleon remained long enough in j Egypt, this great work would have been acj complished. The expense of its construction was estimated at about 15.01)0.000 francs The junction of the Mediterranean and Red Sea, by a canal through the Isthmus of Suez to one ol the mouths ol the .Sue, would bring back the conmicrc ; between India and Europe, to its ancient route along tiia Mediterranean and the Arabian Colt. Alexandria, Venice, and Genoa, w old then again rise to something ol their former splendour, and the benefits ol commerce lie more equally distributed tlian at present Mohammed Alt ia constantly tailing ol making a canal or rail road across th>- Isthmus, but there is no reason to believe that be will ever put his plans in execution. His financed are in such a disordered state at present, and bis resources so much diminished by the loss of Sy ria and I Palestine, that he has no longer any means j for the purpose. The introduction of steamers on the lied Sea has much shortened the journey from England to India. Travellers can now leave England every fortnight in a steamer direct for Alexandria, arriving there in about 10 days. Hence they take the canal to Atfe. on the Nile; there they find a little steam boat

to carry them to Cairo, which they reach in three days from Alexandria. The desert is crossed to Suez, in three days, with camels, or in sixteen hoots by light waggons. The steamer departs lor Bombay, on the arrival of mails Infln England. The þÿw hole journey from England to India has been made, by this route, in thirty two days. Suez stands upon a point of land which runs out for some distance into the sea. þÿ Vessels ol deep draught are obliged to anchor five miles below the town in consequence of

a bank of shoals which there crosses the gulf. The sea runs up for several miles inland above Suez. It is here contracted into a narrow arm, at low tide not more than half a mile broad. Upon leaving Suez, we sent the camels around the head of this part of the sea, while we crossed directly over in a boat, and rejoined them about five hours after their departure. upon the opposite shote. In crossing, we could see the bottom of the sea in all parts. High tide as it was, it appeared to be of no great depth. At l"W tide, the sea is here fordable, as was proved by Dr Madden, who walked from shore to shore. General Bonaparte also essayed to ford the sea at this point. He had proceeded about half of the way across, when the tide returned with such rapidity as to render it impossible for him any longer to keep his seat in the saddle. A tall stalwart soldier seized him, and placing him on his shoulders, made his way for the shore, sustaining himself as well as possible by holding on to the tail of the þÿguide horse. s Before he readied the shore, the water came up to his arm pits, and a few minutes more ol delay, and the death of one man would have changed the destinies of the world ! þÿ 'The whole party escaped in safety, but the horse of Napoleon was drowned. Many years afterwards, Bonaparte, writing fiom St. Helena, thus alludes to this event þÿ þÿ Taking advantage of the low water, 1 crossed the Red Sea dry shod. Returning, 1 was overtaken by the night, and lost my wav in the rising tide. 1 was in the most imminent

danger, and very nearly perished in the same manner as þÿI haroah Had I done so, the event would have afforded to all the preachers of Christianity a magnificent text against þÿrue. Here, we were satisfied, was the scene the miraculous passage ol the Red Sea by the children of Israel. Here the sea is more than ten miles wide, and is of great depth þÿ Another pypolhesis fixes the passage a few miles further up the gulf, where a bank of shoals at low tide lie uncovered almost from shore to shore. But the weight of evidence hears more strongly m lavour of the narrow arm opposite Suez. Here they perceived Pharnah coming down upon them in pursuit. The Israelites immediately broke up their camp, and made for the edge of the sea. Here. þÿ Moses stretched out ins hand over the sea, and the land caused the sea to go back by a strong Fast, wind all that night, and make the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. And the children ot Israel went into the midst of the sea upon drv ground, and the waters were a wall unto them upon the right and left þÿ At certain stages of the tide the sea is fordable at this point, but the passage is dangerous from the sudden and rapid return of the tide. Now, if we suppose the wind to have blown strong from the North East for sometime before the Israelites attempted the passage, the waters must have undoubtedly been driven out ol this shallow arm of the sea, opposite Suez, while the upper part, which is broader and deeper, would retain its waters. Thus, the waters

would be divided and serve as a wall or defence. The Israelites seized the favouroble moment of the recession ol the sea, and passed safely over. A sudden return of the tide, and change of wind, when Pharoah was crossing brought hack the accumulated waters with tremendous violence, and covered the chariots, the hot semen, and all the host of Phaiouh lliut came into the þÿsea.

In in degree was the force of the Divine interposition weakened by this explanation of the Passage on natural eauses. Divine Wisdom conducted the chosen people of God to the Sea at this favourable moment. It was the breath of the Almighty that swept the waters from beneath the Children o| Israel, and which stayed their fury as they foamed on either side: It was the same power that brought back the angry flood, and overwhelmed beneath it the host of þÿ1 haroah- þÿ With the blast of thy nostrils, the waters were gathered together, the floods stood upright as an heap, and the depths were congealed into the heart of the sea." þÿ Thou þÿdid st blow with thv wind ; the sea covered them ; they sank as lead into the mighty þÿwaters. 1 E. (PROM A CORRESPONDENT ) Animal magnetism has, for some years, amused and bewildered the lovers of the marvellous Ridiculed a- a mere illusion or delusion, it has nevertheless perplexed the scientific ; its effects ate too palpable to be denied. hut any rational solution of the cause or causes in which they have originated has hitherto eluded detection, The honour of unveiling this mystery was reserved for Mr. James Hraid, an eminent surgeon in Manchester. who, having witnessed the recent expertinents of Monsieur Lafoiitaine, in the Athenteum of that town, determined, if possible, to bring the system to the test of physiological and anatomical principles. This gentleman, having satisfied his own mind that he could produce the phenomena without personal contact , and even induce sleep when in a different room from the person to he thrown into a stale of somnolency, announced a public lecture on the subject, which he delivered at the Manchester Athenaeum on Saturday last, before seven hundred persons. Mr. Braid lirst placed on a table a common black wine bottle, in the mouth of which was a cork having a plated top. The individual on whom the experiment was to be performed was seated on a chair, and directed to gaze intently at the cork without winking or averting the eyes. The cork was about two feet from the person operated upon, whose head was inclined backwards, forming with the object an angle of about forty-five degrees. In this position he remained for about five minutes,

when profound sleep was produced. The second experiment was completed in the same time, la the third case, a bandage was placed round the head, for the purpose of retaining in an immoveable position a common bottle cork, a little above the root of the nose, as the object to be gazed at, and in about four minutes a complete state of somnoleney ensued. In this case was proved the inability of the patient to open the eyelids, although consciousness was in no respect suspended, as lie was able to reply distinctly to nnv question. T he fourth either through the noise that prevailed, or owing to the person not fixing his gaze con. tinuoiisly on the object. The filth was successful, and although the party made a desperate effert to open his eyes, so much so as to

'r.S3T2«ra>SS2R. agitate his whole frame, they remained as though hermetically scaled; when Mr. Braid took from his pocket a wooden ruler and drew the end of it gently over the upper evelids of both eyes, when the spell was broken, and the sense of sight restored with perfect ease. þÿ These experiments fully demonstrated that the phenomena were perfectly independent of animal magnetism, as tn no one instance w as there the least approach personal contact to or any manipulation. Having thus convinced the audience that sleep could fie produced without pressure <>t the thumbs or waving of the hands, as employed by Monsieur f.afontaine, Mr. Braid proceeded to explain the rationale of his discovery. As 1 am unacquainted with phy siology or anatomy, 1 am not able to do full justice to his theory, but I believe the following account faithfully embodiesits leadingfeatuies. The artificial mode of producing sleep is to fatigue the rectus and levator muscle of the eye, which is affected by a continuously strained and intent gaze at an object viewed under anaoute angle. Under such circumstances, the irritability of those muscles becomes exhausted, as vveli as the irritability of the optic nerve ; giddiness ensues, a mist rises up before the eve, and sleep ensues. Congestion is induced in the eyes, and carried from them to the optic and muscular nerves of the eye, and owing to their proximity to the origin of the nerves of respiration and circulation, affect them through sympathy, and enfeeble the action cf the heart and lungs. The

heart, thus acting feebly, is unable to propel the blood with sufficient force to the extremities, and hence there coldness The blood consequently is accumulated in the region of the heart, and it is thus stimulated ; and in order to remove the inotdinate load, it is corn pelled to increase the frequency of its contractions. in order to compensate lor the feebleness of ns efforts. The brain, head, and face now become congested in consequence, and varied phenomena, resulting from ii regularity in the circulation of tfiat important or gan the brain follow. The inability to raise the upper eyelid Mr. Braid accounts lor on the principle of temporary paralysis of the levator muscles, owing to excessive and long continued exertion at the commencement oi the operation.

RAPACITY OF THU CARRION CROW. On Saturday last a hungry crow pounced upon one of a brood of young Turkics in the pasture at Prospect Hill, while surrounded Lv the larger flock. Eyeing the descent of the enemy, the tuikies immediately surrounded the crow and put him to death. Lord Rat. ms, in his sketches of the History Man, of relates several instances of social defence of the more harmless classes of animals against the common enemy. LATE NEWS FROM CHINA. Latest from Canton. þÿ The Swedish brig Albion, Captain Holdt, arrived yesterday from Canton, having left Macao on the 17th of September ; thus bringing accounts 'about three weeks later than we had before received VVe annex extracts of letters from both Canton and Macao, which give fuller information than we find in the papers which have reached us The British Naval force have, it would seem, in consequence of some hostile movements on the part of the Chinese, imaginary or real, destroyed some villages bordering on the river which leads to Canton, the Chinese apparently offering no resistance, indeed they seem incapable of any, and to be entirely at the mercy of the invaders. Meantime, the British expedition, which had proceeded Northward, had captured \rnoy. and some accounts say, again taken possession of Chusan Amoy is represented to have been a place of considerable strength, at least mihe opinion of the Chinese, and to have contained vast quantities of naval and military stores. It is, however, still twelve hundred miles from Pekin. The Editor of the Canton Press thus speculates on their further proceedings; þÿ Chinhae and Ningpo, we doubt not, will be visited by the fleet, to atone for the murder of Capt. Stead of the Pestnnjee Bomanjee, and if after this it proceeds to the Yang tsze-kiang, and is able to interrupt the communication between it and the great canal, the presence of the enemy cannot fail to be severely felt in the Capital, which will soon find itself without

the usual receipt of salt and grain, the two articles most necessary to its immense population. The presence of the British armament near the canal, would also endanger the safety of several important cities, such as Tchingkiang too, just opposite to where the canal enters the river, and Nanking at no great distance, the second city of the Empire, and still considered by the Chinese an earthly paradise. Every thing that is costly, rare or beautiful, is by the generality of the Chinese considered to come from Nanking ; and although no longer the Capital of an Empire, its populousness and liches, increased by trade and manufactures, are still very great. It may for these reasons, therefore, not be unjustly supposed, that should the British armament take a position commending the canal, the great danger to which the capital, from starvation, and other large cities from the immediate vicinity of an enemy, are exposed, may dispose the Peking Government to a speedy settlement of the question by treaty.

From the New York Weekly Express- hr tt a, January 8, 1842 MOVEMENTS OF THE þÿ þÿILLUSTRIOUS. On Friday morning the steamboat France went down to the Quarantine ground, to receive the luggage of the new Governor General of Canada, Sir Charles Bagot, and lay alongside the 74 the whole of the morning for that purpose. No less than forty-two tons were hoisted on board, among which were two English carriages At about one þÿo clock the Hercules came down to the vessel þÿ the Frances having taken her freight on board, and dropped astern, to allow the other steamer to take her place. þÿ At this moment the stripes and stars were run up to the fore top-gallant mast of the Illustrious, and a salute of 21 guns was fired with great precision and 111 fine style. The Hercules then went alongside, carrying ths

American and British ensigns on her flag-staff, and the Union Jack at her bow. In about half an hour, Sir Charles and suite, left the ship, the marines being drawn upon thequar ter deck, preseming arms, the band playing, and the yards manned. As the steamer moved off. the customary salute due dignitaries of Sir þÿCharts rank, was fired, and the two steamboats proceeded to the city. The Staten Island boat ran round the ship, which gave the passengers an opportunity of observing the ceremonies. Lord Morpeth went down to the Island in the eleven o'clock boat, and proceeded immediately on board the Illustrious. He returned with Sir Charles and suite, and landed with h.m at the North Kiver, pier No. 1, at about 3 F. M. The Hercules in coming up, had besides the flags already mentioned, a large white ensign, with an immense crown in its centre.

A number of persons were at the wharf when the party landed, and accompanied them to the Globe. In the retinue of Sir Charles were several well dressed servants in livery, and two or three good looking Englishwomen and their iiusbands, who belong to the Governor's manege. A fine cutter from the Navy Yardt with a lug-sail, was passed on her way down with some messages of courtesy to Captain Erskine, from the Commander of this station. She made a beautiful appearance, and weathered the blow, which was very fresh, in a gallant manner. The Illustrious is rather a small vessel for her rate, and was built in 1803. She has a high old fashioned poop deck, stern gallery, round full bow, and is much wider at her water line than on deck. She carries 74 guns, some of them 68 pounders, and draws about 24 leet water. She has a crew of 700 men, but they are rather green, and not of the first class of seamen. Her officers are very good looking gentlemanly men, and quite a number of them came up to town yesterday. She sails for Bermuda on Tuesday next' and will probably be visited by numbers before she leaves. She is in no way equal in appearance to the Belle Foule or the North Carolina.
